title: The three quls
hookLine: Ikhlas, Falaq, Nas recited three times morning and evening (Abu Dawud)

cards: Rain coming down hard, a night so dark you can't see your own hand. A small group of men go out looking for the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, hoping he'll lead them in prayer. They find him.
One of them, Abdullah ibn Khubayb, tells what happened next, and Abu Dawud records it. The Prophet turned to him and said one word: say. Abdullah said nothing.
Say. Nothing. A third time: say.
Finally Abdullah asked, what should I say? The answer is three short surahs this path has already met, and a number.

teach.b: The Prophet told him: say Qul huwa Allahu ahad and the two surahs of refuge, three times in the evening and three times in the morning, and they will be enough for you against everything.
Qul is the Arabic for say, and each of the three begins with it. Pickthall: Say: He is Allah, the One! Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of the Daybreak.
Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of mankind. So people call them the three quls, the three says; some also count a fourth, al-Kafirun, which begins the same way. Here's the curious part.
Qul is a command to the Prophet: say this. But when Muslims recite, they keep the word. Not just, He is Allah, the One, but: say, He is Allah, the One.

teach.h: THE COMMAND STAYS IN THE RECITING.
teach.b: The command is part of the revelation, so it stays, and some readers hear each recitation as a return to the moment of being told. Now see how the three fit together.
Al-Ikhlas is about who Allah is: One, needing nothing, with no equal. The Prophet said it equals a third of the Qur'an.

teach.h: WHO YOU TURN TO, THEN WHAT FROM.
teach.b: Al-Falaq and an-Nas are the mu'awwidhatayn, the two refuge-takers: refuge from the dark outside, the envier and the night, and refuge from the whisperer inside.
First, who you turn to. Then, what you're turning away from.
And you met the other practice at the start of this camp: the Prophet would recite all three into cupped hands before sleep and wipe them over his body.

how: In the morning and evening remembrances, al-Ikhlas, al-Falaq and an-Nas are recited three times each, following Abu Dawud's report; before sleep, some recite them into cupped hands, wiping them over the body.

o: say: the word opening three short surahs
go: a call to set out on a journey
wait: a call to hold back and pause

games.q: the three quls — tap the pairs.

s: Muslims drop the word say when they recite these surahs
they keep it: the command is part of the revelation.
the Prophet said al-Ikhlas equals a third of the Qur'an
the practice is once a day, at night
three times each, morning and evening (Abu Dawud).

games.q: it's a dark, rainy night. the Prophet turns to you and says: say. you don't know what he means. what do you do?
o: recite the first thing you know
games.why: Abdullah stayed silent twice, then asked. the answer: the three quls, three times morning and evening (Abu Dawud).

practice: Rest your hands open on your knees and picture the day's two edges, stepping out in the morning and coming back in at night: what would you like to be held by as you go out, and kept from as you come home?
If you pray, you can recite the three quls now, once each, slowly, and again three times tonight; if you don't, sit with the first line, He is One, on each breath.

wordCard.voice: Qul, say: the word that opens al-Ikhlas, al-Falaq and an-Nas, the three surahs recited three times at morning and at evening.

carryVoice: Your line: three times, three. Three short surahs, at both edges of the day. Until tomorrow.
